solution.explanation: 12% of each total: Indore 744 (cars 650, no); Nagpur 672 (850, yes); Coimbatore 840 (1,000, yes); Lucknow 912 (700, no); Vadodara 660 (1,200, yes). So 3 cities.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 misses Coimbatore (14.3%); 4 includes Indore (10.5%); 1 counts only Vadodara, the clear leader.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many candidates from Mandya passed the test?

solution.concept: Passed = appeared × pass percentage
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,260 is the number who failed; 870 is the girls who passed; 1,800 is Tumakuru's figure.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many girls from Udupi passed the test?

solution.concept: Girls who passed = appeared × pass % × girls' %
solution.why_others_wrong: 612 is the boys who passed; 880 takes 55% of all 1,600 who appeared; 1,360 is everyone who passed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which district had the largest number of boys passing the test?

solution.concept: Boys who passed = passed × (100 − girls' %)
solution.explanation: Boys passed: Kolar 936, Hassan 702, Mandya 870, Tumakuru 990, Udupi 612. Tumakuru is the largest.
solution.why_others_wrong: Kolar is second (936); Mandya had the most candidates but only half its passes were boys; Udupi has the highest pass rate but the fewest boys passing.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the overall pass percentage of the five districts taken together (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Overall rate = total passed ÷ total appeared — not the average of the five rates
solution.why_others_wrong: 71% is the simple average of the five pass rates, which ignores the different numbers appearing; 30.88% is the overall fail rate; 47.38% is the girls' share of all who passed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much more water did Ward 4 receive than Ward 3?

solution.concept: Read the two bars and subtract
solution.explanation: Ward 4 received 120 ML and Ward 3 72 ML. Difference = 48 ML.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 ML compares Ward 4 with Ward 2 (96); 36 ML compares Ward 5 (108) with Ward 3; 12 ML compares Ward 4 with Ward 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many wards received more water than the average supply per ward?

solution.concept: Average = total ÷ number of wards; then compare each bar
solution.explanation: Total = 84 + 96 + 72 + 120 + 108 + 60 = 540 ML, so the average is 90 ML. Wards 2 (96), 4 (120) and 5 (108) are above it: 3 wards.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 misses Ward 2, which is only 6 ML above the average; 4 includes Ward 1 (84); 1 counts only the tallest bar.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ward 6 has a population of 40,000. What was the average water supply per person per day in Ward 6 in June? (June has 30 days; 1 ML = 10 lakh litres.)

solution.concept: Per person per day = monthly supply ÷ population ÷ days
solution.explanation: Ward 6 received 60 ML = 6,00,00,000 litres. Per person: 6,00,00,000 ÷ 40,000 = 1,500 litres in the month, or 1,500 ÷ 30 = 50 litres a day.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,500 litres is the monthly figure; 48.39 litres divides by 31 days; 5 litres treats 1 ML as 1 lakh litres.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Wards 1 and 5 lose 15% of their supply to leakage, and every other ward loses 10%. How much water actually reached consumers in the six wards in June?

solution.concept: Apply each loss rate to its own wards' supply
solution.explanation: Wards 1 and 5 received 84 + 108 = 192 ML and lost 15% = 28.8 ML. The other wards received 348 ML and lost 10% = 34.8 ML. Delivered = 540 − 63.6 = 476.4 ML.
solution.why_others_wrong: 486 ML applies 10% to every ward; 459 ML applies 15% to every ward; 468.6 ML swaps the two rates.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In July, supply to every ward rises by 15% over June, except Ward 4, whose supply falls by 30%. By what percentage does the total supply to the six wards change from June to July?

solution.concept: Compute July's total from each ward's own change; percentage changes cannot simply be averaged
solution.explanation: Five wards other than Ward 4 had 420 ML; +15% gives 483 ML. Ward 4: 120 × 0.7 = 84 ML. July total = 567 ML against 540 ML in June: an increase of 27 ML = 5%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Increases by 15%' ignores Ward 4's fall; 'increases by 7.5%' averages the six percentage changes; 'decreases by 15%' subtracts 30 from 15.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The total buffalo milk collected from the four villages is what percentage of the total cow milk collected?

solution.concept: Add each series across the villages, then divide
solution.explanation: Cow milk = 14 + 9 + 16 + 11 = 50 thousand litres. Buffalo milk = 8 + 12 + 6 + 14 = 40 thousand litres. 40 ÷ 50 = 80%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 125% divides the other way; 44.44% is buffalo milk's share of all milk; 20% is how much less buffalo milk there is.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which village did buffalo milk form the largest share of that village's total milk collection?

solution.concept: Compare buffalo ÷ (cow + buffalo) for each village
solution.explanation: Buffalo shares: P 8/22 ≈ 36.4%, Q 12/21 ≈ 57.1%, R 6/22 ≈ 27.3%, S 14/25 = 56%. Village Q is highest.
solution.why_others_wrong: Village S has the most buffalo milk but also more cow milk, so its share (56%) is just below Q's; P and R have much lower shares.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The cooperative pays ₹42 per litre for cow milk and ₹58 per litre for buffalo milk. How much did it pay Village S for the week's milk?

solution.concept: Price each kind of milk separately; the bars are in thousand litres
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,26,000 swaps the two prices; ₹12,50,000 uses the average price ₹50 for all 25,000 litres; ₹14,50,000 pays the buffalo-milk price for all of it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Cow milk contains 4% fat and buffalo milk 7% fat. If all the milk collected from the four villages is mixed together, what is the fat percentage of the mixture?

solution.concept: Fat % of a mixture is the quantity-weighted average of the fat percentages
solution.explanation: Fat = 50 × 4% + 40 × 7% = 2 + 2.8 = 4.8 thousand litres in 90 thousand litres of milk, so 4.8 ÷ 90 = 5⅓%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.5% is the simple average of 4% and 7%; 5⅔% swaps the quantities (50 of buffalo milk, 40 of cow milk); 4.8% is the fat in thousand litres, not a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much did the start-up spend on technology in 2025-26?

solution.concept: Amount = percentage × total
solution.explanation: Technology is 15% of ₹48 crore = ₹7.2 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹15 crore reads the percentage as crore; ₹5.76 crore is content (12%); ₹9.6 crore is marketing (20%).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By how much did spending on salaries exceed the combined spending on marketing and rent?

solution.concept: Subtract the percentages first, then convert to rupees
solution.explanation: Salaries 35% against marketing + rent = 20% + 8% = 28%. The gap is 7% of ₹48 crore = ₹3.36 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹7 crore leaves the gap as a percentage; ₹7.2 crore subtracts content + rent (20%) instead of marketing + rent; ₹11.04 crore subtracts only rent (27%).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the central angle of the sector for marketing?

solution.concept: Central angle = percentage × 360 ÷ 100 = percentage × 3.6
solution.explanation: Marketing is 20% of the total, so its angle is 20 × 3.6 = 72°.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20° reads the percentage as degrees; 54° is technology's angle (15%); 36° is the angle for 'Others' (10%).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2026-27 the start-up's total expenditure rises by 25% and its spending on salaries rises by 20%. What percentage of the new total will salaries be?

solution.concept: New share = old share × (1 + salary growth) ÷ (1 + total growth)
solution.explanation: Salaries were ₹16.8 crore; 20% more is ₹20.16 crore. The new total is ₹60 crore. 20.16 ÷ 60 = 33.6%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 35% assumes the share is unchanged; 42% applies only the salary growth; 28% applies only the total's growth.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many hectares are under pulses?

solution.concept: Area = angle ÷ 360 × total
solution.explanation: Each degree stands for 7,200 ÷ 360 = 20 hectares. Pulses have 54°, so 54 × 20 = 1,080 hectares.
solution.why_others_wrong: 900 uses oilseeds' 45°; 1,440 uses rice's 72°; 3,888 reads 54 as a percentage of 7,200.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The area under wheat is what percentage more than the area under rice?

solution.concept: Percentage more can be worked out directly from the angles
solution.explanation: Wheat 108°, rice 72°. The difference 36° is 36 ÷ 72 = 50% of rice's angle, so wheat's area is 50% more.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33.33% divides by wheat's 108°; 36% reads the difference in degrees as a percentage; 150% is wheat as a percentage of rice.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Sugarcane yields 70 tonnes per hectare and vegetables 18 tonnes per hectare. What is the total production of sugarcane and vegetables together?

solution.concept: Convert each angle to hectares, then multiply by that crop's own yield
solution.explanation: Sugarcane: 36 × 20 = 720 ha × 70 = 50,400 t. Vegetables: 27 × 20 = 540 ha × 18 = 9,720 t. Total = 60,120 tonnes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50,760 tonnes swaps the yields; 55,440 tonnes applies the average yield (44 t/ha) to both; 50,400 tonnes is sugarcane alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Next year, one-fourth of the area now under rice is shifted to pulses, and nothing else changes. What will be the ratio of the area under pulses to the area under rice?

solution.concept: Move the shifted area out of one sector and into the other; the total is unchanged
solution.explanation: One-fourth of rice's 72° is 18°. Rice falls to 54° and pulses rise to 54 + 18 = 72°. Ratio = 72 : 54 = 4 : 3.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 4 is reversed; 5 : 4 raises pulses by a quarter of their own area instead of rice's; 79 : 47 shifts 25 degrees instead of 25%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average number of passengers per month over the six months?

solution.concept: Average = total of the six values ÷ 6; the values are in thousands
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,85,000 averages only January and June; 3,30,000 divides by 5 instead of 6; 2,70,000 is March's figure.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which month was the percentage increase in passengers over the previous month the highest?

solution.concept: Percentage change = change ÷ previous month's value; a large absolute rise on a large base can be a smaller percentage
solution.explanation: Changes: Feb −6.25%, Mar +45 on 225 = +20%, Apr +30 on 270 ≈ +11.1%, May −5%, Jun +45 on 285 ≈ +15.8%. March is highest.
solution.why_others_wrong: June has the same absolute rise as March (45 thousand) but on a larger base; April's rise is smaller; May fell.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average fare was ₹38 per passenger in January–March and ₹42 per passenger in April–June. By how much did the fare revenue of April–June exceed that of January–March?

solution.concept: Revenue = passengers × fare for each quarter; both the count and the fare changed
solution.explanation: January–March: 735 thousand × ₹38 = ₹2.793 crore. April–June: 915 thousand × ₹42 = ₹3.843 crore. Difference = ₹1.05 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹68.4 lakh prices the 1,80,000 extra passengers at ₹38 and ignores the fare rise; ₹75.6 lakh prices them at ₹42 only; ₹29.4 lakh is only the effect of the ₹4 fare rise on the first quarter's passengers.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: City X's total rainfall for the five months was what percentage more than City Y's?

solution.concept: Add each line's five values; 'more than Y' uses Y's total as the base
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.09% divides by X's total; 110% is X as a percentage of Y; 100% reads the 100 mm difference as a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which month was the difference between the rainfall of the two cities the largest?

solution.concept: Read the vertical gap between the two lines for each month
solution.explanation: Gaps: June 30 mm, July 60 mm, August 10 mm, September 10 mm, October 30 mm. The largest is July.
solution.why_others_wrong: August is Y's wettest month but the cities differ by only 10 mm; October and June differ by 30 mm.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2026, City X's rainfall in each of these months is 10% less than in 2025, and City Y's is 10% more. By how many millimetres will City Y's five-month total exceed City X's?

solution.concept: A uniform percentage change in every month changes the total by the same percentage
solution.explanation: X's total becomes 1,100 × 0.9 = 990 mm and Y's becomes 1,000 × 1.1 = 1,100 mm. Y exceeds X by 110 mm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 mm applies the 10% changes to the 100 mm gap only; 210 mm adds the old 100 mm gap to the new one; 0 mm assumes a 10% fall and a 10% rise cancel.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many members were on the annual plan?

solution.concept: Members on annual plan = total − monthly − quarterly
solution.why_others_wrong: 300 is the quarterly plan; 240 splits the non-monthly 480 equally; 120 is the number of women on the annual plan.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many women members did the centre have in all?

solution.concept: Apply each plan's own percentage of women and add
solution.explanation: Women: monthly 40% of 360 = 144, quarterly 45% of 300 = 135, annual 2/3 of 180 = 120. Total = 399.
solution.why_others_wrong: 441 is the number of men; 420 assumes half the members are women; 336 applies the monthly plan's 40% to all 840.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many men were on the quarterly plan?

solution.concept: Men = members on the plan − women on the plan
solution.explanation: Quarterly members = 300, of whom 45% = 135 are women, so 165 are men.
solution.why_others_wrong: 135 is the women on the quarterly plan; 216 is the men on the monthly plan; 60 is the men on the annual plan.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Over a full year, by what percentage does staying on the monthly plan cost more than buying the annual plan?

solution.concept: Convert both plans to a yearly cost; 'more than the annual plan' uses the annual cost as the base
solution.explanation: Monthly plan for a year = 12 × 1,500 = ₹18,000. Annual plan = ₹14,400. The extra ₹3,600 is 3,600 ÷ 14,400 = 25%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% divides by the monthly plan's 18,000; 11.11% compares the quarterly plan (16,000) with the annual plan; 125% is the monthly plan's yearly cost as a percentage of the annual plan's.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If every member stays on the same plan for a full year, what total fee will the centre collect in that year?

solution.concept: Convert each plan's fee to a yearly amount before multiplying by the number of members
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,02,72,000 counts only one quarter's fee for quarterly members; ₹1,20,96,000 charges everyone the annual fee; ₹79,32,000 counts only one month's fee for monthly members.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In November, one-fourth of the monthly-plan members switch to the annual plan, and 60 new members join on the quarterly plan; no one leaves. What percentage of all members are then on the annual plan?

solution.concept: Update each plan's count, then divide by the new total membership
solution.explanation: A quarter of the 360 monthly members (90) move to the annual plan, which now has 270. With 60 new quarterly members, the total is 900. Annual share = 270 ÷ 900 = 30%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32.14% divides by the old total of 840; 21.43% is the October share (180 ÷ 840); 20% forgets the 90 switchers (180 ÷ 900).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many packets of cookies did the bakery make that Saturday?

solution.concept: Split 1,500 in the ratio 6 : 2 : 7 (15 parts)
solution.explanation: One part = 1,500 ÷ 15 = 100, so cookie packets = 7 × 100 = 700.
solution.why_others_wrong: 600 is the number of loaves; 560 is the cookie packets sold; 1,050 takes 7/10 of 1,500.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many items in all were left unsold at the end of Saturday?

solution.concept: Unsold = made − sold, for each item
solution.explanation: Unsold loaves = 60, cakes = 30 and cookie packets = 140. Total = 230.
solution.why_others_wrong: 90 counts only loaves and cakes; 1,270 is the number sold; 200 counts loaves and cookies but not cakes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the bakery's revenue from cakes on the Saturday itself?

solution.concept: Revenue = number sold × selling price, counting only that day's sales
solution.explanation: Cakes sold on Saturday = 85% of 200 = 170. Revenue = 170 × 300 = ₹51,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹60,000 counts all 200 cakes; ₹29,750 uses the cost of making; ₹55,500 adds the next morning's half-price sales.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the bakery's total profit on the Saturday's cakes, including the next morning's half-price sales?

solution.concept: Profit = all revenue from the cakes − cost of making all 200 cakes
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹16,000 leaves out the half-price sales; ₹25,750 charges the cost of the 170 cakes sold on Saturday only; ₹25,000 sells all 200 at full price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking all the items baked that Saturday (including those given away, and counting the next morning's cake sales), what was the bakery's overall profit percentage (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Profit % = (total revenue − total cost of everything made) ÷ total cost × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 43.66% leaves out the next morning's cake sales; 33.33% divides the profit by revenue instead of cost; 77.35% counts the cost of only the items sold on Saturday.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was Asha's achievement percentage?

solution.concept: Achievement % = achieved ÷ target × 100
solution.explanation: Asha achieved ₹46 lakh against a target of ₹40 lakh: 46 ÷ 40 = 115%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 86.96% divides target by achievement; 15% is only the excess over 100%; 6% reads the ₹6 lakh excess as a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was Bilal's target?

solution.concept: Target = achieved ÷ achievement %
solution.explanation: Bilal achieved ₹36 lakh, which was 90% of his target, so the target = 36 ÷ 0.9 = ₹40 lakh. (He earns no incentive.)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹32.4 lakh takes 90% of 36; ₹39.6 lakh adds 10% to 36; ₹45 lakh is Deepak's target.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What amount did Deepak achieve?

solution.concept: Work back from the incentive: excess = incentive ÷ 5%
solution.explanation: An incentive of ₹45,000 is 5% of the excess, so the excess = 45,000 ÷ 0.05 = ₹9,00,000 = ₹9 lakh. Achieved = 45 + 9 = ₹54 lakh (120% of target).
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹9 lakh is only the excess; ₹47.25 lakh adds 5% to the target; ₹90 lakh reads ₹45,000 as ₹45 lakh of excess.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total incentive earned by the five executives?

solution.concept: Fill every missing cell first; an executive below target earns nil, not a negative incentive
solution.explanation: Asha: 5% of 6 lakh = ₹30,000. Bilal: below target, nil. Chitra: achieved 112% of 50 = 56 lakh, excess 6 lakh ⇒ ₹30,000. Deepak: ₹45,000. Eshan: target = 63 ÷ 1.05 = 60 lakh, excess 3 lakh ⇒ ₹15,000. Total = ₹1,20,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,05,000 leaves out Eshan; ₹90,000 leaves out Chitra; ₹1,00,000 deducts 5% of Bilal's ₹4 lakh shortfall as a negative incentive.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many students dropped out of the Morning batch?

solution.concept: Dropped out = enrolled − completed
solution.explanation: Morning: 120 enrolled and 100 completed, so 20 dropped out.
solution.why_others_wrong: 56 subtracts the passed students (64) from the enrolled; 36 is the number who completed but failed; 30 is the Evening batch's dropouts.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many students enrolled in the Afternoon batch?

solution.concept: Completed = passed ÷ pass %; enrolled = completed + dropped out
solution.explanation: 54 passed, which is 72% of those who completed, so 54 ÷ 0.72 = 75 completed. Enrolled = 75 + 15 = 90.
solution.why_others_wrong: 75 is the number who completed; 69 adds the dropouts to the passed students; 60 subtracts the dropouts instead of adding them.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking the four batches together, what percentage of all the students who enrolled passed the final test (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Fill all the missing cells, then total passed ÷ total enrolled
solution.explanation: Enrolled: 120 + 90 + 150 + 80 = 440. Passed: Morning 64% of 100 = 64, Afternoon 54, Evening 55% of 120 = 66, Weekend 45 — total 229. 229 ÷ 440 = 52.045…% ≈ 52.05%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 64.51% divides by those who completed (355) instead of those who enrolled; 66.5% averages the four pass percentages; 80.68% is the completion rate (355 ÷ 440).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: 3/8 of 256
Quantity II: 0.45 × 200

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Evaluate each quantity exactly
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 256 ÷ 8 × 3 = 96. Quantity II = 0.45 × 200 = 90. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' compares 3/8 = 0.375 with 0.45 and ignores the different numbers they multiply.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Perimeter (cm) of a square of area 196 cm²
Quantity II: Circumference (cm) of a circle of radius 9 cm (take π = 22/7)

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Square: side = √area, perimeter = 4 × side; circle: circumference = 2πr
solution.explanation: Quantity I: side = √196 = 14 cm, perimeter = 56 cm. Quantity II: 2 × 22/7 × 9 = 396/7 ≈ 56.57 cm. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' comes from using π = 3 (2 × 3 × 9 = 54); '≥' would need the two to be equal.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Speed of the stream (km/h) if a boat goes 30 km downstream in 2 hours and 18 km upstream in 2 hours
Quantity II: 2.5

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Stream speed = (downstream speed − upstream speed) ÷ 2
solution.explanation: Downstream = 15 km/h, upstream = 9 km/h, so the stream = (15 − 9) ÷ 2 = 3 km/h. 3 > 2.5, so Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' halves the difference twice (6 ÷ 4 = 1.5); 'Quantity I ≤ Quantity II' would need the stream to be no faster than 2.5 km/h.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Probability of getting at least one head when three fair coins are tossed
Quantity II: Probability that a number chosen at random from 1 to 50 is not a multiple of 8

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Use complements: P(at least one head) = 1 − P(no head); count multiples of 8 up to 50
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8 = 0.875. Quantity II: multiples of 8 up to 50 are 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48 (6 numbers), so P = 44/50 = 0.88. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' counts 7 multiples of 8 (43/50 = 0.86); 'Quantity I ≥ Quantity II' fails for the same reason, since 0.875 < 0.88.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the speed of the car?
I. The car covers 210 km in 3 hours 30 minutes.
II. The car's speed is 20% more than that of a bus that covers 150 km in 3 hours.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed

solution.concept: A statement is sufficient on its own if it fixes the answer without the other
solution.explanation: I: 210 ÷ 3.5 = 60 km/h — sufficient. II: the bus runs at 150 ÷ 3 = 50 km/h, so the car runs at 1.2 × 50 = 60 km/h — sufficient. Either statement alone answers the question.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' or 'II alone' overlooks that the other statement also gives the speed; 'both together' assumes the two must be combined.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the cost price of the bag?
I. The bag was sold at a profit of 20%.
II. The profit on the bag was ₹150.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Profit % alone or profit alone does not fix the cost; together profit = CP × profit %
solution.explanation: I gives only a percentage, and II only a rupee amount; neither fixes the cost price alone. Together: 20% of the cost price = ₹150, so the cost price = ₹750.
steps: I alone: any CP with 20% profit
II alone: ₹150 profit on any CP
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' and 'II alone' each leave the cost price open; 'not sufficient even together' misses that the two combine into one equation.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both statements I and II together are needed

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What is the length of the train?
I. The train crosses a signal pole in 12 seconds.
II. The train crosses a 300 m long platform in 27 seconds.
III. The speed of the train is 72 km/h.

options.text: Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
Only I and II together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary

solution.concept: Check each pair; each statement alone links length and speed but cannot fix both
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Only I and II' misses the other two working pairs; 'III alone' gives the speed but not the length; 'all three' is more than needed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Any two of the three statements together are sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the area of the right-angled triangle?
I. Its hypotenuse is 13 cm.
II. Its perimeter is 30 cm.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed

solution.concept: With the hypotenuse c and perimeter P known, a + b = P − c and a² + b² = c², so ab (and the area) is fixed
solution.explanation: I alone: many right triangles have hypotenuse 13 (5-12-13 has area 30; 7.8-10.4-13 has area 40.56). II alone: 5-12-13 and 7.5-10-12.5 both have perimeter 30, with areas 30 and 37.5. Together: a + b = 17 and a² + b² = 169, so 2ab = 289 − 169 = 120 and the area = ab/2 = 30 cm².
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' assumes the triangle must be 5-12-13; 'either' assumes the same for the perimeter; 'not sufficient' misses that a + b and a² + b² together fix ab.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are needed
